reading.title: Reading appearance and aroma notes
reading.text: The student interprets a fictional sensory report without tasting a sample. Color describes its appearance; clarity concerns cloudiness, and viscosity concerns resistance to flow. Legs are trails of liquid on a glass, not proof of quality or sweetness. Rim here means the edge of the liquid's visible color, not the glass's physical rim. Opacity concerns how much light passes through. Hue describes the color family; depth its intensity, and brilliance its visual brightness. Sediment means settled particles. Aroma, bouquet and nose are smell-related descriptors whose usage can vary. Floral and fruity describe impressions resembling flowers or fruit rather than prove an ingredient was added. The report gives the intended sense of each word. A photograph cannot establish an aroma or independently verify the written assessment.

reading.title: Interpreting sensory comparisons
reading.text: The report describes earthy, spicy, herbaceous, mineral and oaky impressions. These are comparisons with familiar smells or flavors, not statements that soil, spices or stones were added. Body concerns perceived weight or fullness. Tannin can contribute astringency; acidity and sweetness concern different properties. Finish describes the impression remaining after tasting, while balance concerns the relation among components. Complexity concerns multiple interacting characteristics. Structure concerns their overall relationship, and mouthfeel concerns tactile sensations in the mouth. Length describes how long the impression persists rather than a physical distance. The student asks which part of the written report supports a claim. These subjective descriptors can differ among assessors. The exercise practices understanding a report and does not require consumption or rank a product's quality.

reading.title: Separating descriptors from menu pairings
reading.text: The student compares words in a fictional menu discussion. Dry concerns low residual sugar under the relevant classification; sweet concerns greater sweetness. Crisp suggests fresh acidity, smooth suggests a gentle texture, and velvety compares texture with velvet. Bold and delicate describe different intensities, while rich concerns concentration. Light and full-bodied concern perceived body rather than the bottle's weight. Cheese pairing, meat pairing, seafood pairing and dessert pairing name proposed flavor combinations, not universal rules. An appetizer is a small opening food course. The student asks whether the description concerns sweetness, texture, body or the meal. Preference and dietary needs can affect a pairing. The class interprets terminology without recommending a product, requiring alcohol consumption or claiming that every assessor will experience the same qualities.

reading.title: Understanding a menu's organization
reading.text: A hospitality worksheet presents a fictional menu. The main course is the meal's principal dish. A palate cleanser is a neutral food or drink intended to reduce lingering flavors between different items. A tasting menu presents several small courses. A wine flight is a group of small samples arranged for comparison, whereas a cheese board is a serving board holding cheeses. The learner can describe the arrangement without ordering or tasting anything. The class asks how the menu could accommodate a request for an alcohol-free alternative and clear dietary information. Availability and suitable substitutions depend on the venue. The worksheet teaches vocabulary and polite questions; it does not establish the contents, allergens, age suitability or safety of an actual menu item.
